chapters.title: Chapter 1: Pricing a Bond from Its Cash Flows

lessons.title: Premium, Par, and Discount: What the Price Tells You About the Coupon

children.text: Scroll through the G-Sec list on RBI Retail Direct and you will see bonds priced at ₹92, others at ₹100 and others at ₹107, all issued by the same Government of India. Many investors read ₹92 as "cheap" and ₹107 as "expensive". That is the wrong instinct. In a liquid market, a bond's price above or below ₹100 is not a bargain or a rip-off; it is a precise message about how its coupon compares with today's market yield. This lesson teaches you to read that message, and to avoid the most common high-coupon trap in Indian fixed income.

body.text: A bond's price adjusts until every buyer earns the market yield. A premium price is the market charging you for an above-market coupon; a discount price is the market paying you for a below-market one.

children.text: The Three-Way Rule

markDefs.definition: A bond trading above its face value, because its coupon rate is higher than the current market yield.
A bond trading at exactly its face value, because its coupon rate equals the current market yield.
A bond trading below its face value, because its coupon rate is lower than the current market yield.

children.text: In Lesson 2 you repriced a 7.10% bond at different yields and saw the pattern. Here it is as a rule you can apply instantly to any fixed-coupon bond. A bond trades at a
premium
when its coupon is above the market yield, at
par
when the two are equal, and at a
discount
when its coupon is below the market yield. The rule works in reverse too: if you see a price above ₹100, you know the coupon is higher than the yield without calculating anything.

body.caption: Three 10-year bonds from the same issuer, all priced at a 7.00% market yield (per ₹100 face value)

children.text: How do these situations arise in India? A bond's coupon is fixed at issue, but yields move for years afterwards. The 6.10% GS 2031 was auctioned in 2021, when RBI had cut the repo rate to 4% during the pandemic. When yields later rose above 7%, that 6.10% coupon became a below-market coupon, and the bond fell to a discount. Older G-Secs issued with coupons above 8% in the early 2010s went the other way and traded at premiums once yields fell below their coupons.

body.title: Classify without calculating
body.question: Comparable G-Secs currently yield 6.60%. Which of these illustrative bonds will trade at a discount?
body.explanation: Only the 5.85% bond has a coupon below the 6.60% market yield, so it must trade below ₹100. The 7.30% and 8.15% bonds trade at premiums, and the 6.60% bond trades at par (assuming the same yield applies at each maturity).

children.text: How Big Should the Premium Be?

There is an elegant shortcut. A premium bond pays you an extra slice of coupon, above what a par bond would pay, every period until maturity. The premium is simply the present value of those extra slices. For the 7.10% bond at 6.80% from Lesson 2, the extra coupon is (7.10% − 6.80%) ÷ 2 × ₹100 = ₹0.15 per half-year, for 10 half-years, discounted at 3.40%.

body.caption: c = coupon rate, y = market yield, m = coupons per year, n = periods left. For the 7.10% bond: ₹0.15 × 8.3587 = ₹1.25, matching the ₹101.25 price. A negative answer is a discount.

children.text: This formula reveals two things. First, the size of the premium or discount depends on the coupon gap: a bigger gap means a bigger deviation from ₹100. Second, it depends on the number of periods left: the same coupon gap produces a larger premium on a long bond than on a short one, because there are more extra coupons to value.

body.title: Use the premium shortcut
body.prompt: An illustrative PSU bond pays an 8.20% coupon semi-annually and has exactly 4 years left, priced on a coupon date. Comparable bonds yield 7.40%. Using the shortcut, what is its premium over ₹100 per ₹100 face value? Round to two decimal places.
body.explanation: Extra coupon per period = (8.20% − 7.40%) ÷ 2 × ₹100 = ₹0.40. Annuity factor at 3.70% for 8 periods = (1 − 1.037⁻⁸) ÷ 0.037 = 6.8169. Premium = ₹0.40 × 6.8169 = ₹2.73, so the price is ₹102.73.

children.text: Pull to Par: Every Bond Ends at ₹100

markDefs.definition: The tendency of a bond's clean price to move towards face value as maturity approaches, even when market yields do not change.

children.text: Whatever a bond trades at today, on its maturity date it is worth exactly ₹100. So, with yields unchanged, a premium bond must lose value every year and a discount bond must gain value every year until both reach face value. This is called
pull to par
. The shortcut formula explains the path: as periods remaining shrink, there are fewer extra (or missing) coupons to value, so the premium or discount shrinks with them.

body.title: Pull to Par: Three Bonds at a Constant 7.00% Yield (₹ per ₹100 face value)

body.text: If you own a premium bond, expect its price in your RBI Retail Direct or demat holdings statement to drift lower every year, even if interest rates never change. That is not a loss in the economic sense. It is the premium you paid being returned to you, piece by piece, through the higher coupons. Selling a premium bond in a panic because "the price keeps falling" is a classic retail mistake.

children.text: Different Routes, Same Return

Now the key insight. Hold the 8% premium bond and the 6% discount bond from the table above for one year, with the yield staying at 7.00%, and reinvest the first half-year coupon at 3.5% for six months. Their returns arrive in completely different shapes, but they end up identical.

body.caption: One-year return at a constant 7.00% yield (per ₹100 face value)

cells: Coupons, with the first reinvested for six months

stats.label: Premium bond
stats.context: High coupon income, small price loss

stats.label: Discount bond
stats.context: Lower coupon income, small price gain

children.text: Both bonds return exactly 7.1225%, which is the 7.00% market yield compounded half-yearly. The coupon only changes how the return is split between income and price movement, never its total. That total is the yield to maturity, which is where Chapter 2 begins.

body.title: Premium Bonds vs Discount Bonds at the Same Yield

columns.label: Premium bond (coupon above yield)
points: More of the return comes as coupon income, paid out along the way
Clean price drifts down towards ₹100 over time
More cash back early, so slightly less sensitive to interest rate changes
Coupons are taxed as income every year, even though part of each one only returns your premium

columns.label: Discount bond (coupon below yield)
points: More of the return comes as a price gain, received at sale or maturity
Clean price drifts up towards ₹100 over time
More cash back late, so slightly more sensitive to interest rate changes
Part of the return is a capital gain rather than yearly interest income, which can change the post-tax outcome

body.title: Where every bond ends
body.textWithBlank: At a constant market yield, both premium and discount bonds move towards ___ as they approach maturity.
body.explanation: Every bond repays its face value at maturity, so the premium shrinks and the discount narrows over time. This is pull to par.

body.title: The 9% coupon trap
body.scenario: Rohit Khanna, a business owner in Ludhiana, has ₹5 lakh to put into government-guaranteed bonds for five years. His relationship manager shows him two illustrative bonds of the same issuer, both maturing in exactly five years and paying semi-annual coupons: Bond A has a 9.00% coupon and is priced at ₹106.16; Bond B has a 6.50% coupon and is priced at ₹95.89. Rohit says: "Obviously Bond A. 9% is much better than 6.5%."
body.prompt: Work out what yield each bond is priced at, explain whether Rohit's reasoning holds, and name the factors that could genuinely make one better than the other for him.
body.modelAnswer:
1. Check the prices at a 7.50% yield: Bond A (9.00%) discounts to ₹106.16 and Bond B (6.50%) to ₹95.89. Both are priced at the same 7.50% yield to maturity.
2. Bond A pays ₹9 a year per ₹100 face value but will repay only ₹100 on a ₹106.16 purchase, losing ₹6.16 through pull to par. Bond B pays ₹6.50 a year but gains ₹4.11 as it rises from ₹95.89 to ₹100.
3. So the 9% coupon is not a 9% return. At these prices both bonds are expected to return the same 7.50% a year, compounded half-yearly, if held to maturity and coupons are reinvested at that yield.
4. Real differences that could matter for Rohit: (a) Tax: Bond A delivers more of its return as coupon income taxed at his slab rate every year, while Bond B delivers more as a price gain, which is taxed differently; for a high-slab taxpayer this can make Bond B better after tax. (b) Cash needs: if Rohit wants regular income, Bond A provides more of it. (c) Reinvestment: Bond A returns more cash early, so it depends more on the rates available to reinvest coupons. (d) Rate sensitivity: Bond B, with more cash at the end, will move slightly more if yields change before he sells.
5. The right comparison is always yield to maturity, then post-tax return and cash flow fit, never the coupon rate alone.

children.text: Split any bond's coupon into two pieces: the coupon a par bond would pay at today's yield, plus the extra (or missing) amount. The first piece, together with the ₹100 face value, is exactly a par bond, so it is worth exactly ₹100 today. The second piece is a stream of equal payments for n periods, an annuity, and its present value is the payment times the annuity factor. Add the two: price = ₹100 + present value of the coupon gap. When the coupon is below the yield, the gap is negative and so is the adjustment, giving a discount.

content.latex: P = 100 + \underbrace{\frac{(c - y) \times 100}{m} \times \frac{1 - (1 + y/m)^{-n}}{y/m}}_{\text{PV of the coupon gap}}
content.caption: Holds for pricing on a coupon date. Between coupon dates, the same idea applies to the dirty price.

points: Coupon above market yield means premium, equal means par, below means discount. The price tells you the relationship instantly.
A premium or discount is not a bargain or a rip-off; it is the market equalising returns across bonds with different coupons.
Premium or discount = present value of the coupon gap. Bigger gaps and longer maturities mean bigger deviations from ₹100.
Pull to par: at a constant yield, premium bonds drift down and discount bonds drift up, reaching ₹100 at maturity.
An 8% premium bond and a 6% discount bond priced at the same 7% yield both returned 7.12% over a year; only the mix of income and price change differed.
Never compare bonds on coupon rate. Compare yield to maturity first, then tax, cash flow needs and rate sensitivity.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment or tax advice. Bonds, prices, yields and investors are illustrative unless named, and returns shown are before tax and costs. The tax treatment of coupon income and capital gains on bonds depends on factors such as listing status and holding period, and tax rules change, so consult a chartered accountant or a SEBI-registered investment adviser before acting.
